POPULATION ECOLOGY

  • Population Ecology is the study of populations in relation to environment.
  • Population size: Number of individuals in a defined geographic area which is governed by:
  • Natality (birth rate)
  • Mortality (death rate)
  • Immigration (entry into population)
  • Emigration (exit from population)
  • Dispersion is a pattern of spacing among individuals within the geographic boundaries. Three types of Dispersion are — Clumped, Uniform, Random
  • Biotic Potential: Maximum reproductive capacity under optimal conditions.
  • Carrying Capacity: Maximum sustainable population size in an environment.
  • Limiting Factors: Environmental variables that restrict population growth.

Life history Strategies

  • These strategies describe how organisms adapt their reproductive and developmental traits to different environmental conditions and resource availability.
Featurer-selected speciesK-selected species
SizeSmallLarge
ReproductionMany offsprings, short timeFew offsprings, long time

ECOSYSTEM

  • The term "Ecosystem" was coined by "Sir Arthur George Tansley" in 1935.
  • An ecosystem is a functional unit where living organisms interact with each other and their physical environment.
  • It was described as the basic unit of ecology by Francis C. Evans in 1956 (Science 123: 1127–1128).
  • Ecosystems provide the following services:
  • a) Provisioning Services: Direct material benefits like food, water, wood, fuel.
  • b) Regulating Services: Help maintain ecological balance like air/water quality, flood control, pollination.
  • c) Supporting Services: Enable other services (e.g., habitats, genetic diversity).
  • d) Cultural Services: Non-material benefits (e.g., recreation, spiritual value).

TERRESTRIAL ECOSYSTEM

  • Land-based ecosystems involving interaction of biotic and abiotic components in a given area.

Subdivisions of Terrestrial Ecosystem are:

  • a) Forest Ecosystem
  • b) Grassland Ecosystem
  • c) Desert Ecosystem
  • d) Tundra Ecosystem

DEFORESTATION

  • Deliberate clearance of forests is known as Deforestation.
  • Causes for deforestation:
  • Shifting cultivation
  • Development projects
  • Fuel needs
  • Raw material demands
  • Effects of Deforestation on Ecosystem:
  • Lower groundwater levels
  • Reduced precipitation
  • Soil erosion
  • Landslides

DESERTIFICATION

  • Continuous degradation of dry land ecosystems due to climate change and human activity is called Desertification.

AQUATIC ECOSYSTEM

Aquatic Organisms

Classification of Aquatic Organisms:

  • Neuston: Float / attached to the upper surface of water
  • Periphyton: Attached to submerged surfaces (e.g., Algae, Cyanobacteria)
  • Plankton: Phytoplankton → autotrophs (e.g., algae); Zooplankton → freely floating and bottom dwelling (e.g., crustacean, Protozoa)
  • Nekton: Organisms capable of active locomotion (e.g., fish, squid)
  • Benthos: Bottom dwelling organisms (e.g. crabs, mollusks)

Factors affecting Productivity in Aquatic Habitats

  • SunLight:
  • Photic Zone: Upper layer where light enables photosynthesis
  • Aphotic Zone: Deeper layer, where light penetration is restricted, hence, limited to respiration only.
  • Dissolved Oxygen (DO):
  • Cold water holds more oxygen than warm water.
  • DO below 3-5 ppm can harm aquatic life

TYPES OF AQUATIC ECOSYSTEM

  • Aquatic ecosystems are categorized based on the nature and movement of water.

1. Lentic Ecosystem

  • Still water bodies like lakes, ponds, and swamps.
  • Also known as lacustrine ecosystems.
  • Productivity influenced by nutrient content, light penetration, and depth.

2. Lotic Ecosystem

  • Flowing water systems such as rivers and streams.
  • Known as riverine ecosystems.
  • Well-oxygenated and nutrient-rich; organisms adapt to water currents.

3. Marine Ecosystem

  • Saltwater environments like oceans and seas with salinity ≥35 ppt.
  • Cover over 70% of Earth's surface.
  • Include diverse habitats like estuaries and coral reefs.
  • Dominated by producers such as phytoplankton and algae.

CORAL REEF

  • Coral reefs are complex underwater structures formed by colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps, which are related to jellyfish and sea anemones.
  • Each polyp secretes a calcareous exoskeleton, which remains after it dies and serves as a base for new polyps.
  • Over time, this leads to the formation of large reef structures.

Ideal Conditions for Coral Growth:

  • Shallow, sunlit waters (up to 30 meters deep)
  • Warm temperatures (typically 25–30°C)
  • Clean and clear saline water
  • Low nutrient levels (corals thrive in oligotrophic conditions)
Can you recall the phylum of Corals?

TYPES OF CORAL REEFS

  • Fringing Reefs: Closest to the shoreline, directly attached to land.
  • Barrier Reefs: Separated from land by a lagoon; typically found further offshore.
  • Atoll reefs: An atoll is a ring-shaped coral reef that encircles a central lagoon, but no central island is visible above sea level.

Threats to Coral Reefs:

  • Global Warming: Leads to temperature rise and coral stress
  • Coral Bleaching: Expulsion of symbiotic algae due to heat
  • Ocean Acidification: Increased CO₂ makes seawater more acidic, weakening coral skeletons
  • Pollution and Sedimentation: Reduce light penetration and smother coral
  • Natural Disasters: Storms and tsunamis can break coral structures

Coral Reefs in India:

  • Gulf of Mannar
  • Andaman & Nicobar Islands
  • Lakshadweep Islands
  • Gulf of Kutch

ESTUARIES AND MANGROVES

ESTUARIES

  • The Region where rivers meet the sea
  • Form a transition zone i.e. a. ecotone between freshwater and marine ecosystems
  • Mostly rich in: diatoms, dinoflagellates, green & blue-green algae

MANGROVES

  • Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees (halophytes) that grow in coastal intertidal zones, especially in tropical and subtropical regions.
  • They act as a transitional zone (ecotone) between land and sea.
  • With their dense root systems, mangroves stabilize shorelines, reduce erosion, and serve as natural barriers against storm surges and tsunamis.
  • They thrive in saline, waterlogged, and oxygen-poor soils.

Functions:

  • Produce Pneumatophores: Aerial roots that facilitate breathing in anaerobic soil.
  • Viviparous in nature: Seeds germinate while still attached to the parent tree.
  • Salt Excretion/Filtration: Roots filter salt or excrete it via leaves.
  • Helps in carbon sequestration, storing more carbon per hectare than most other forests
  • Support biodiversity and act as buffers against extreme weather events

WETLANDS

  • Wetlands are Transitional lands between aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems.
  • They act as ecotones and buffer zones.
  • Examples: Chilika Lake, Keoladeo Ghana
  • Montreux Record: A list of 48 endangered wetlands. India's Keoladeo National Park of Rajasthan and Loktak Lake of Manipur are on that list.

Challenges in Aquatic Ecosystems

Eutrophication

  • Eutrophication: A process by which a water body becomes overly enriched with nutrients, resulting in oxygen depletion and excessive algae growth.

Types of Eutrophication

  • Natural Eutrophication: Gradual aging of lakes via nutrient accumulation.
  • Cultural Eutrophication: Accelerated by human activity (e.g., fertilisers, sewage discharge etc.)

Effects of Eutrophication

  • Algal bloom
  • Oxygen depletion - due to which the Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) increases.
  • Decline in aquatic biodiversity

Algal Bloom

  • It refers to the rapid increase of algae population in a water body.

Effects of Algae bloom:

  • Toxin production
  • Creation of dead zones (Hypoxia)
  • Harmful to humans and animals
Hypoxia: Very less oxygen concentration in a water body for living organisms to survive.
